The correlations above are computed over the full prior range. Participants classified as

have estimates of precision weighting between 1.5 and 3.5 (5th to 95th percentile). Among the 206 recovery simulations with a true precision weighting in this range, the correlations are .86 for noise reactivity and .95 for the switch probability. Among the 95 simulations in which all six true values lie within the participants’ 5th to 95th percentiles, they are .81 and .95. The low recovery of noise reactivity is concentrated at low precision weighting (.64 in the lowest third of the prior range), where participants are not found.

The correlation between the estimate of one parameter and the true value of another does not exceed .21 in absolute value; the largest values occur between noise reactivity and belief momentum (.21 and .15). Within posteriors, noise reactivity and belief momentum are negatively correlated (mean correlation −.64), and noise reactivity and the switch probability weakly so (−.33). The two parameters of the first pair are therefore not determined independently of each other for a single participant, although their estimates are nearly unconfounded across participants.

Why the commitment gain was changed

children.label: Why the commitment gain was changed

children.value: The commitment gain determines how strongly the allocation commits to the more probable state (see
). Three observations led to the change from 8 to 3.
Participants place nets at the other state’s direction.

For each session, the nets within ±2 slots of the direction of the other latent state and of a matched third direction were counted on stable regular trials (trial in episode above 4, no oddball on this or the previous trial). The 62 participants classified as

place a median of 0.41 more nets at the other state’s direction than at the third direction (interquartile range 0.17 to 0.90; 87% of participants above zero). The difference is present in every instruction condition (medians 0.41, 0.60 and 0.17). A corresponding difference for the direction in which oddballs land is absent (median 0.08).
With gain 8, the simulated agent does not.
For parameters drawn from the priors, the median difference is 0.08 with gain 8, 0.26 with gain 4, 0.44 with gain 3 and 0.73 with gain 2. Gain 3 matches the participants’ median and quartiles.
A lower gain makes the switch probability and noise reactivity more identifiable.

With a lower gain, the allocation carries graded information about the state belief, on which both parameters act. A screen with a feature-based regression (4,000 simulations per gain) and the trained networks agree on this (table above).

Reading the share inside the interval.

The predictive intervals reflect only the simulation variability of one session at the participant’s posterior and are narrow relative to the differences between participants: their median width is 0.6 to 0.8 between-participant standard deviations for the main summaries of the level of behaviour. A small systematic offset therefore places many participants outside the interval. Two further quantities describe the fit more directly: the offset in units of the between-participant standard deviation, and the rank correlation between observed and predicted values across participants, which shows whether the differences between participants are reproduced.

The offset is the median of observed minus predicted values. Across the 53 features with between-participant variance, the offset is below half a between-participant standard deviation for 29 and reaches one standard deviation for 4 (standard deviation of the trial-to-trial shift, belief lability, standard deviation of the angular error, oddball recovery speed). The rank correlation is at least .70 for 18 features and at least .50 for 31; the features with low rank correlations are mostly difference scores and slopes with little reliable between-participant variance (for example the odd-even episode difference and the defense-rate slope). For the main summaries of behaviour, the fitted agent thus reproduces the differences between participants closely, and the deviations are offsets shared by the participants. Shared offsets do not affect analyses of individual differences in the parameters.

A trial-level comparison locates the difference. On stable trials, participants’ allocations are centred on the target with a smaller spread than the agent’s (10.6° against 13.7°), and they are centred on the other state’s direction more often (6.4% of trials against 2.7%). The agent instead produces more allocations that are centred on no structured direction (21% against 10%). After an oddball, participants centre their allocation on the location where it landed on about 20% of the following trials, in both states; the agent does so on 8%. Trial-to-trial shifts above 90° make up 19% of participants’ stable trials and 10% of the agent’s, while a quarter of participants’ shifts are below 5° (agent: 14°).

Participants thus alternate between precise placements and discrete moves to a small number of locations, whereas the agent represents all off-target placements by a Gaussian shift of the allocation. Across participants, the estimated placement noise correlates with the share of allocations centred on the other state’s direction (Spearman

The agent is a low-dimensional description of behaviour along six interpretable dimensions. It reproduces the level and the between-participant ordering of the main behavioural summaries and not every placement. Its parameters are read as measures of these dimensions.
